what: Numbers the README states that were measured against a file this repository does not distribute. Everything else in the README comes out of public/model/meta.json and is held to it by check:claims. These cannot be recomputed here, so they are pinned here instead: the file they came from, its hash, and the command that produced them. check:upstream asserts that every percentage in the README is either a meta.json claim or one of these, so a number cannot sit in prose unaccounted for again.
why: Deleting a true and useful number to satisfy a rule about reproducibility is the wrong trade. A reader is better served by "97.28 looks better than it is, the floor is 74.98" than by 97.28 alone. What the rule is really for is that a number cannot drift silently, and pinning it here gets that without losing it.

numbers.says: predicting O for every word scores this, because most words carry no slot
numbers.method: Count the gold word tags in the evaluated rows and take the share that are O. 54,472 of 72,652, which is 74.98 percent. 39.64 percent of rows carry no non-O tag at all.
numbers.whyItIsHere: meta.json records accuracy but not the tag distribution, so the baseline cannot be computed from anything this repository ships. Adding it to meta.json would mean re-running tools/quantize.py, which needs the checkpoint and the test set, and neither is obtainable.
numbers.closesIfEverObtainable: tools/quantize.py evaluate() writes the tag distribution into meta.json, check:claims covers it, and this entry is deleted.
